themes.definition: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) template, the guidance for completing it and the worked examples that central government provides so that public bodies can publish a record of an algorithmic or AI tool (starting codes: templates and information, serving publication and registration).
themes.what_is_set_out: The ATRS is the resource most often supplied for the publication side of accountability: eight documents point to it. UK086 provides the template itself, in an Excel and a Google Sheets version, with section-by-section guidance and fictional worked examples; the UK087 workbook sends users to that guidance for help completing it; UK085 supplies worked formats, including how to show in a published record that a field is withheld and why ('EXEMPT: National security'; a second example cites a statutory section, the location text is cut off). UK099 describes the ATRS as a template for public sector organisations to document and share how and why they use algorithmic tools, and (coder note) as a way to publish fairness metrics and testing activity; UK174 recommends using it to tell the general public about AI solutions, saying it is particularly relevant where the tool is used directly or indirectly in decision-making (coder note); UK190 (DWP) sends staff to section 3.4 of the ATRS guidance for its logging and exemption rules; AI_Insights names it, and elsewhere (coder note) calls it the 'algorithmic transparency and reporting standard'. The documents disagree on who provides it: CDDO and CDEI in UK139, the Government Digital Service in UK086 and UK085, the Algorithmic Transparency Team (ATRS team) in UK087, and no one in UK174, UK099, UK190 and AI_Insights [inference: this tracks the standard moving between government bodies over time]. They also differ on its force: UK174 presents use as a recommendation, while UK268, in the part of its UK section reported in the coder note to UK-ACC-RES-026, describes the ATRS as 'now mandatory for central government departm[ents]'.
themes.holders: Provided by: CDDO & CDEI (UK139); Government Digital Service (UK086, UK085); the Algorithmic Transparency Team / ATRS team (UK087); provider not named in UK174, UK099, UK190 and AI_Insights. Used by: 'you', government departments and public sector organisations (UK174); public sector organisations (UK099); DWP and its staff (UK190); no user named in the AI_Insights passage.
themes.binding: The template and guidance are provided; no obligation attaches to them in these passages. UK174 recommends use in an imperative practical recommendation ('Use existing standards and recording mechanisms such as the ATRS'), which is not statutory and has no stated consequence. The duty to publish itself sits in the Accountability/Design cell; within this cell only UK268's reported description (coder note) calls the ATRS mandatory for central government departments. No passage says what happens if a record is not completed or is wrong.
themes.checks: n/a as a check. The template is a publication aid. UK099 (coder note) says a record can carry fairness metrics and testing activity, but the passages do not say what a tool is compared against, which metric or threshold is reported, who verifies a record, or what follows from it.

themes.definition: The places where information about AI tools, their data or their code is made public: the GOV.UK repository of ATRS records and its record finder, data.gov.uk, and open source practice for code (starting codes: tools and access, serving publication).
themes.what_is_set_out: UK086 says that completed ATRS information is published on the GOV.UK repository as an ATRS record, and the UK087 workbook links to a browser 'record finder' for published records (the coder note adds that its metadata sheet refers to filtering and searching). UK085 says that when a record is updated, 'This update will be reflected on the published record on GOV.UK', so the channel carries revisions, not only a one-off publication. UK099 points to data.gov.uk as the place to publish government datasets, following the Open Data Charter (coder note). AI_Insights tells developers in government who use AI coding assistants to follow unnamed 'open source guides' when coding in the open (coder note: this supports its coding-in-the-open entry). No passage says who runs the repository [inference: GDS or the ATRS team], how long records stay up, whether records of withdrawn tools are marked, or whether the public can respond through it.
themes.holders: GOV.UK repository: provider not named (nearest named actor the ATRS team or GDS [inference]); record finder: ATRS team (UK087); data.gov.uk: provider not named ([inference] UK government); open source guides: provider not named, followed by developers in HMG (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: Channels are provided, not required, in these passages. UK099 is permissive ('You can publish'). AI_Insights uses 'should' for following open source guides; not statutory; consequence not stated.

themes.theme: Records kept as evidence for answering
themes.definition: Records, documentation formats and record-keeping functions that an organisation keeps so that it can later explain or justify what it did with an AI tool to complainants, auditors or the public.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK216, addressed to public bodies in England and non-devolved and cross-border bodies, says under a checklist item headed 'Keep a clear record of how…' (cut off in the input) that keeping these records 'can also help you' respond to complaints, audits and freedom of information requests: records are presented as the information that makes later answering possible. AI_Insights, on using AI to manage shared drives, says government knowledge and information management professionals 'may therefore need' tooling that records the actions taken to dispose of drives, folders or items, including scope and extent, reasons and authorisation (coder note). UK174 points to data and model cards or fact sheets, with Google's as an example, as a reference when documenting AI models and the data used in training and testing, and to the process-based governance framework in national ethics and safety guidance that helps project teams document proportionate governance actions. The documents differ in what is recorded: decisions and reasons (UK216), disposal actions and who authorised them (AI_Insights), models and data (UK174), governance steps (UK174). None says how long records are kept, who may see them or who checks them.
themes.holders: Public bodies in England, and non-devolved and cross-border public bodies (UK216); 'you', government knowledge and information management professionals (AI_Insights); project teams (UK174); Google named as an example source of card formats, and the author of the ethics and safety guidance not named (UK174).
themes.binding: Good practice (UK216: 'can also help you'); conditional (AI_Insights: 'may therefore need'); resources provided or pointed to (UK174). Not statutory; no consequence stated. The duty to keep records is coded in other cells (coder note to UK-ACC-RES-031: Delivery/Design).
themes.checks: These are records, not checks. Trigger: not stated (AI_Insights: when disposal actions are taken). Compared against: not stated; data and model cards (UK174) document the data used in training and testing, but the passages do not say what testing is done or against what. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: project teams; knowledge and information management professionals; public bodies. What happens with the result: records are used to answer complaints, audits and freedom of information requests (UK216).

themes.theme: Guidance on explaining AI-assisted decisions and on transparency
themes.definition: Guidance and standards that tell organisations how to explain AI-assisted processes and decisions to the people affected, or how to make AI systems transparent; chiefly the ICO and Alan Turing Institute guidance 'Explaining decisions made with AI'.
themes.what_is_set_out: The ICO and Alan Turing Institute guidance is the single resource named most often in this cell: UK174, UK099 (twice), UK010, UK139 (twice) and UK207 all point to it. It is described as giving organisations practical advice to explain the processes, services and decisions delivered or assisted by AI to the individuals affected by them (UK099, UK139, UK207), and UK174 calls it the UK's national AI explainability guidance, which (coder note) sets out six types of explanation and documentation processes. Most documents only point to it; UK010 (Ofgem) goes further, saying organisations 'should also ensure' that consumers are informed about the use of data relating to them, 'In line with' that guidance. Attribution differs: UK099 at p.12 and UK010 name the ICO alone, while UK174, UK099 at p.62, UK139 and UK207 present it as co-produced with the Alan Turing Institute. Beyond it, UK136 points to a Royal Society policy briefing on explainable AI (a non-state source), and UK139 lists technical standards: IEEE 7001 on transparency of autonomous systems, and ISO/IEC TS 6254 (explainability) and ISO/IEC CD 12792 (transparency taxonomy), both under development (coder note).
themes.holders: Provided by the Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute (UK174, UK099 p.62, UK139, UK207; the ICO alone in UK099 p.12 and UK010); the Royal Society (UK136); IEEE and ISO/IEC (UK139). Used by organisations generally; in UK010, organisations processing data using AI.
themes.binding: Pointers to non-binding guidance and voluntary standards. The only obligation attached is UK010's 'organisations should also ensure that consumers are informed', framed as in line with the guidance; no consequence is stated in that passage (Ofgem points to its enforcement guidelines separately, UK-ACC-RES-041).
themes.checks: n/a. The passages do not say how an explanation is checked against what the tool actually did.

themes.theme: Guidance and advice on legal duties, rights and enforcement
themes.definition: Guidance from regulators, and advice from inside the organisation, on how existing law (data protection, equality, rights about automated decisions, sector enforcement) applies to AI and whom it holds to account.
themes.what_is_set_out: Regulators are the main source. The ICO's guidance on AI and data protection is pointed to for people in compliance-focused roles (UK206) and, in UK139's annex, as explaining how to interpret data protection law for AI systems that process personal data, including security risks and data minimisation (coder note). UK086 points to the ICO's guidance on 'Rights related to automated decision making, including profiling' for completing the ATRS field on appeals and review. UK139 lists the Equality and Human Rights Commission's guidance on use of AI by public bodies, which its annex describes as about meeting Public Sector Equality Duty obligations (coder note); it is the only equality-law resource in the cell and the only regulator guidance here written for public bodies specifically. UK010 (Ofgem) points to its own Enforcement Guidelines for how it enforces. UK139 is the only passage in which issuing such resources is itself the action asked for: regulators are to 'Issue tools and guidance' to AI developers and deployers on how the laws apply to AI 'and whom those laws can hold to account'. Inside the organisation, UK099 says the data protection officer or information assurance team 'should be able to advise' on data protection obligations.
themes.holders: Information Commissioner's Office (UK206, UK139, UK086); Equality and Human Rights Commission (UK139); Ofgem (UK010); regulators generally as issuers, with AI developers and deployers as recipients (UK139); the organisation's data protection officer (DPO) or information assurance team (UK099).
themes.binding: Guidance is provided or pointed to. UK139's 'Issue tools and guidance' is a non-binding ask of regulators; UK099's 'should be able to advise' is an expectation that internal advice exists, not a duty. No consequence is stated for not using the guidance or for regulators not issuing it.

quotes.quote: Issue tools and guidance to AI developers and deployers to communicate clearly how these laws apply in the context of AI and whom those laws can hold to account.

themes.theme: Outside audit, certification and accreditation support
themes.definition: Bodies and standards outside the public organisation that can give or underpin independent assurance of AI: the ICO's audit consultation, UKAS accreditation services and an ISO/IEC standard for audit and certification bodies (starting code: outside support, serving audit).
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 says the ICO 'also offers AI auditing consultation and support to government organisations' and refers readers to the ICO's guide to AI audits (coder note); this is the only direct offer of outside audit help to government bodies in the cell. UK206 names the United Kingdom Accreditation Service as a supporting stakeholder whose services 'include certification, testing, inspection and calibration', without saying whether any public body must use them. UK139 lists ISO/IEC DIS 42006, requirements for bodies that audit and certify AI management systems, as currently under development, alongside ISO/IEC 38507 on governance of AI for members of a governing body and ISO/IEC 25059 on quality models (coder note). The three differ in kind: a regulator's service, an accreditation body's services, and a draft standard that would govern certifiers.
themes.holders: Information Commissioner's Office (UK174); United Kingdom Accreditation Service (UK206); ISO/IEC standards bodies (UK139). Recipients: government organisations (UK174); not stated (UK206, UK139).
themes.binding: Offered or mentioned only. No passage requires a public body to obtain outside audit or certification, and no consequence is stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated. Compared against: not stated for the ICO and UKAS; for ISO/IEC 42006, requirements for AI management systems [inference: a check on an organisation's management system, not on a tool's outputs]. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the ICO (consultation and support); UKAS; certification bodies under ISO/IEC 42006. What happens with the result: not stated. UKAS 'testing' is not said to include testing AI outputs.

themes.theme: Purpose-built audit catalogue, helper tool and fairness metrics
themes.definition: Tools made specifically for auditing AI in government: the catalogue and Excel Audit Helper Tool co-produced by six national audit offices, and the list of fairness metrics given to auditors (starting code: tools and information, serving audit).
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 is material co-produced by the national audit offices of Brazil, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK; the NAO's page offers its catalogue and helper tool 'to support the assurance of AI in government'. The Audit Helper Tool is an Excel workbook of detailed audit questions and the audit evidence to look for, ordered by stage of the AI lifecycle; the NAO page adds that it sets out the controls auditors should expect across AI-related risk areas (coder note). The workbook itself was not extracted for coding (coder note), so its questions are not in these passages. Appendix 3 gives auditors fairness metrics for classification systems: true and false positive rates, precision and negative predictive value, group fairness definitions such as equal opportunity, statistical parity, equalised odds and sufficiency, and individual-level measures (coder note); the list is explicitly 'not exhaustive' and 'a starting point for the auditor'.
themes.holders: Provided by the National Audit Office with the audit offices of Brazil, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Norway; used by auditors.
themes.binding: Provided tools; no obligation to use them and no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: an audit of an AI system; when audits happen is not stated, though the helper tool's questions follow lifecycle stages. Compared against: the controls auditors should expect (helper tool) and fairness definitions (Appendix 3). Metric or threshold: classification error rates broken down by group (true positive rate, false positive rate, precision, negative predictive value) and group fairness criteria; no thresholds are given and the list is a starting point. Who: auditors in supreme audit institutions. What happens with the result: not stated in these passages (UK268 elsewhere aims at 'meaningful recommendations for improvements', UK-ACC-RES-016). This is the only place in the cell that names quantitative measures applied to an AI tool's outputs.

quotes.quote: The Audit Helper Tool is an Excel tool that contains detailed audit questions and related audit evidence that auditors can look for in an AI system audit, ordered by steps along the AI lifecycle.

themes.theme: International and other-field sources of audit criteria
themes.definition: Standards, guidelines and tools from outside UK government that UK268 points auditors to as criteria for judging an AI system, especially where AI-specific criteria are lacking.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268 directs auditors to international standards and guidelines for judging whether AI is used safely and ethically; per the coder note its section 3.2 names the OECD AI Principles, the US NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the EU High-Level Expert Group's ethics guidelines and a Fraunhofer IAIS assessment source (the note is cut off). Where AI-specific requirements are missing, auditors 'should look to established standards and requirements from related fields': German BSI IT security standards, ISACA's COBIT, and cloud catalogues (BSI C5 and AIC4, the Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix). It also names national data protection authorities' guidance (the ICO, Norway's Datatilsynet, a German data protection body, and Brazil's data protection law per the coder note), and the HLEG ethics guidelines as 'a blueprint for developing audit criteria for ethical AI grounded in basic human rights', citing Norway's audit office's use of the European Convention on Human Rights and the Norwegian Constitution (coder note). The European Commission's compliance checker is pointed to for estimating which EU AI Act provisions apply to a system. The criteria offered concern IT security, cloud controls, data protection and ethics; most are non-UK, and several come from non-state bodies (ISACA, the Cloud Security Alliance).
themes.holders: Users: auditors. Providers: German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), ISACA, the Cloud Security Alliance, national data protection authorities (ICO, Datatilsynet and others), the EU High-Level Expert Group on AI, the European Commission; per the coder note also OECD, NIST and Fraunhofer IAIS.
themes.binding: Pointers: 'should look to' (good practice, UK-ACC-RES-011) and 'can' elsewhere. Nothing binding; no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: an audit; timing not stated. Compared against: these external standards and guidelines, used as audit criteria. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: auditors. What happens with the result: not stated. None of the named sources is described as covering the accuracy or consistency of AI outputs.

themes.theme: UK government guidance named as audit references
themes.definition: UK government and UK regulator guidance that UK268 points auditors to as statements of best practice for purchasing, deploying, analysing, evaluating, approving and assuring AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK268's UK section points auditors to the AI Playbook for the UK Government (best practice in purchasing and deploying AI), the white paper's principles (what best practice 'might look like' when deploying AI; the five principles per the coder note), the AQuA Book (robust analysis; per the coder note also assurance factors, risk and impact assessment, bias and compliance audits), the Magenta Book (impact evaluation of AI interventions) and AI procurement guidelines. As 'existing guidance for the approval and assurance of AI' it lists the government's Introduction to AI assurance, the Financial Reporting Council's 'AI in Audit' and digital and technology spend control (Risk and Importance framework). All are framed as things auditors 'can use' to understand best practice, not as binding criteria. [inference] On these passages an auditor of a UK public body has no single statutory UK AI standard to audit against: the UK sources offered are guidance, while the same section reports the ATRS as mandatory for central government departments (coder note to UK-ACC-RES-026).
themes.holders: Users: auditors. Providers: UK government (AI Playbook, white paper, AQuA Book, Magenta Book, AI procurement guidelines, Introduction to AI assurance, spend control); Financial Reporting Council; the National Cyber Security Centre is also named in the holder field of UK-ACC-RES-027, but what it provides is cut off.
themes.binding: Pointers ('Auditors can use this guidance'). Non-binding; no consequence stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: an audit; timing not stated. Compared against: these guides as best practice; the coder notes say the AQuA Book covers risk and impact assessment and bias and compliance audits, and the Magenta Book impact evaluation, but no method, metric or threshold is given in the passages. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: auditors. What happens with the result: not stated.
